newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel split on Rhone-Poulenc vaccine.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel split on Rhone-Poulenc vaccine.

text.p: An advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Thursday said it had concerns about compromised immunity with Pasteur Merieux Connaught's combination vaccine for diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (DPT) and haemophilis B influenza (HIB).
Connaught is a subsidiary of Rhone-Poulenc Rorer.

The panel was unanimous that the vaccine was as safe and effective as the separate vaccines, but said that it appears that infants might not have the same immunity to HIB as when it is given separately.

Panel chairwoman Patricia Ferrieri of the University of Minnesota said that given the public health need for such a combination vaccine the FDA and Connaught should try to address committee concerns as soon as possible.
The FDA is not bound by its committees' advice but usually follows it.

The Connaught vaccine, to be sold as TriHIBit, uses the safer "acellular" form of pertussis. It is the first DPT vaccine to also include HIB, and is meant for the first three shots in a four-part immunization series, for infants 2, 4, and 6 months old.
TriHIBit was approved in the U.S. in September 1996 for the final shot in the series, for toddlers aged 15 to 18 months.

The panel's discussion focused on infants' antibody response to TriHIBit's HIB component. "There certainly is some evidence of interference," said panelist Thomas Fleming of the University of Washington, noting that based on the data, it was hard to say that infants' immunity to HIB was not being compromised.

HIB has always been given separately as, historically, the immune response to the component has been low when part of a combination. Before the early 1980s, when an HIB vaccine was first introduced, the disease was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in infants. Since that time, HIB disease has largely been controlled.

In studies involving 4,300 infants, TriHIBit was shown to be as safe and effective as the DPT and HIB vaccines given separately, said Connaught.The FDA agreed that there were "no clinically relevant" differences between the two regimens. In infants receiving TriHIBit, there were two seizures overall, and some increased incidence of hospitalization, which the panel wanted studied further after the vaccine is introduced.

Combination vaccines have been eagerly awaited by both physicians and parents as they promise to reduce the time and expense of immunization, and trauma to infants. The first combination DPT vaccine with an acellular component, made by Wyeth-Lederle, a unit of American Home Products, was approved in 1991. Subsequent acellelular DPTs, made by Connaught and SmithKline Beecham, were approved in 1996.
Wyeth-Lederle hopes to gain approval for its combination DPT/HIB vaccine as well. The firm filed for FDA approval for the combination, to be sold as Tetracel, in March.
